column4: This rainstorm's darkness, thunder, and lightning presents the cloud's frightening face; it contrasts with the section's cloud as rain-bearing growth and mercy, though the storm here serves as a simile.
The section links rain to growth on earth; this ayah compares good giving to a garden on high ground that yields twice when heavy rain falls, with even light rain sufficient.
The section joins cloud, water, and provision in Moses' journey; this ayah gives Moses' people shade from cloud and twelve springs for drinking, each with a known drinking place.
The section connects ground, water, and plant growth; this ayah places rivers and paired fruits in the spread earth, a concrete landscape where water and yield meet.
The section describes layered, heavy cloud; this ayah shows lightning and raises heavy clouds, with fear and hope accompanying the weather.

The section's ن ع م dictionary gloss describes life's freshness and goodness; this ayah says God's نعمة cannot be counted, following the rain, crops, rivers, and other provisions described in 16:10–17.
The section links water drawn from earth to useful growth; this ayah describes a garden of grapes and palms with crops between them, in the paired garden scene continued at 18:33.
The section brings water together with plant yield; this ayah says both gardens produce fruit and have a river running through them, continuing the garden scene of 18:32.
The section treats water as what sustains people and livestock; this ayah makes the link more basic by saying God created every moving creature from water.
The source section gives رَبَب a secondary dictionary sense of sweet water; this ayah names one sea as fresh and sweet and contrasts it with salty, bitter water.
The section joins rain to soil's growth; this ayah sends water from the sky and brings out fruits of varied colors.
The section describes earth made productive by water; this ayah says God made gardens of palms and grapes and caused springs to gush within them, following dead land revived in 36:33.
The section links growth and gathered water to provision; this ayah says people eat the fruit of the gardens and notes that they did not make it themselves, completing 36:34.
The section's cloud and rain renew the land; this ayah names the alternation of night and day, provision from the sky, winds, and the revival of dead earth as signs.
The section pictures rain leaving green growth on soil; this ayah asks people to consider what they sow, immediately before asking who makes it grow in 56:64.
The section says a rain-bearing cloud grows plants; this ayah asks whether people make their crops grow or God does, continuing the sowing question in 56:63.
The section names a tender plant that does not wither in summer; this ayah says God could make the crop dry into fragments, the reversal of enduring green growth.

The section's و س م dictionary entry describes the first rain stamping earth with vegetation; this ayah uses the same source root in سَنَسِمُهُ for a punitive mark on a person's snout, reversing the earth's beneficial green mark.
The section describes a well as a source of drinkable water; this ayah describes a spring from which God's servants drink and which they cause to flow.
The source section's secondary رَبَب gloss calls water sweet; this ayah names fresh, sweet water given to drink, alongside the earth's firm mountains.
The section's rain grows useful plants; this ayah adds thick gardens to the grain and plants in 78:15, all following water poured from clouds in 78:14.
The section says water comes from earth through a well and supports growth; this ayah explicitly says God brought out the earth's water and its pasture.
The section's rain and well water serve people and animals; this ayah calls the pasture and other provisions enjoyment for people and their livestock, completing 79:31–32.
If the sky's "return" here evokes recurring rain, it pairs with the earth's fissure in 86:12, recalling the section's rain-to-soil growth; that reading is an echo, not an explicit well scene.
The section says rain leaves growth on earth; this ayah swears by the earth's fissure, paired with the sky's return in 86:11.
